parts.title: A new way to measure what people describe feeling: using it to compare the visions people see under psychedelics
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Introduction

Psychedelics are substances such as LSD, psilocybin, mescaline and DMT that can change how we see the world in striking ways. But we still don't know how much the visual effects of one psychedelic differ from those of another. The effects of any single psychedelic can vary a great deal, both from one person to the next and within the same person. To answer this question with enough precision, we need a very large collection of reports in which people describe what they actually saw.

Methods

We carried out an observational study, which means we studied reports that people had already written, rather than giving anyone a drug ourselves. We used the huge Erowid collection of experience reports, in which people describe their own experiences with substances. We analyzed reports about 103 different substances that affect the mind. The middle value (the median) was 217 reports for each substance. Thirty of these substances are usually called psychedelics, and the other 73 served as substances to compare them with.

To turn these written descriptions into numbers, we used a tool from OpenAI that turns each sentence into a list of numbers, called a vector, that captures its meaning. We then trained a computer program, called a classifier, to recognize which sentences described visual effects, based on those numbers.

Results

The share of sentences that described visual effects differed between substances, and these differences were statistically significant and consistent, even among the psychedelics themselves. (A difference is called statistically significant when a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone if there were really no difference.) We then sorted the visual effect sentences from the psychedelics into types of effect, such as movement, color or pattern. Again, we found statistically significant and consistent differences.

Discussion

Overall, our findings show that different psychedelic substances reliably differ in how likely they are to affect vision, and in the kinds of visual effects they produce.

Keywords: psychedelics, substances that affect the mind, how we see, visual effects, computer analysis of language, Erowid, large language model (LLM), what people describe feeling
parts.introduction_first: Changes in how we see are among the most well-known features of psychedelic substances. LSD and psilocybin are two "classical psychedelics" that have been given to human volunteers in research studies (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016; Griffiths et al., 2006). Many other psychedelic substances are also valuable tools for research (Shulgin and Shulgin, 1997; Shulgin and Shulgin, 1991).
parts.conclusion:
Conclusion

There is still a lot we need to learn about how psychedelics change what we see. Inside our brain, nerve cells pass messages to each other using chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. These messengers attach to docking points on the surface of nerve cells, called receptors, and each type of receptor responds to a particular messenger. We still need to understand how the strength of activation of different receptor types and subtypes contributes to what we see, and how psychedelics act on these receptors to change our experience. On top of that, we still know very little about how psychedelics work at the level of groups of connected nerve cells and larger brain networks.

Even so, knowing how strongly a substance attaches to receptors, or how it affects single nerve cells, is not enough to fully explain how psychedelics change what we see and how we think. A convincing explanation of how psychedelics affect brain activity must describe more than their actions on single nerve cells. It must also explain how changes in the patterns of activity across large groups of nerve cells are linked to changes in what we see and how we think.

This second question is still a mystery. However, several theories are being developed to explain how psychedelics affect seeing and thinking in the short term, and how they affect personality, our view of the world and mental health over the long term (Carhart-Harris and Friston, 2019; Vollenweider and Preller, 2020). Our study adds to this work by showing that we need to take into account the roles that many types of receptors play in brain activity.

Finally, our study suggests that psychedelics can be useful tools for studying basic questions in psychology and neuroscience. One example is how patterns of activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes what we see, relate to different features of what we see. Future studies could compare measures such as how substances attach to receptors, brain activity and people's descriptions of their experiences across many psychedelic substances. This could help untangle the many different biological causes behind the wide range of things we see while we are awake.
parts.introduction_rest:
Each psychedelic has its own particular chemical structure, and because of this, different psychedelics affect the brain in different ways. If different psychedelics also change what we see in their own typical ways, then comparing their effects on the body with what people describe feeling would be a powerful way to study how the brain produces what we see while we are awake. Yet how the visual effects of one psychedelic differ from those of another is still largely an open question.

From what people have told us informally, the visual effects of even a single psychedelic can vary widely from one person to the next. So an experiment in which researchers give psychedelics to human volunteers would probably not be precise enough to answer this question. In this study, we tackle the question by studying reports that people have already written, rather than giving anyone a drug ourselves. We made use of the huge Erowid collection of experience reports.

The Erowid Center keeps a public archive of experience reports, written by users and available on its website, in which people describe their own experiences with substances that affect the mind. In our study, we analyzed reports about 103 different substances. The middle value (the median) was 217 reports for each substance. Thirty of these substances are generally recognized as psychedelics, and some of them are also called hallucinogens. The other 73 served as substances to compare them with. They include sedatives (substances that calm people down), stimulants (substances that make people more alert and active), herbs and other kinds of drugs.

We counted a substance as a psychedelic if two things were true. First, the Erowid experience reports described it as a psychedelic. Second, it either belonged to one of three chemical families, called tryptamines, phenethylamines and lysergamides, or it contained substances from these families.

To analyze these written descriptions with numbers, we turned each sentence into a vector, a list of numbers that captures the sentence's meaning. We used a tool from OpenAI called text-embedding-ada-002 (Greene et al., 2022) to create a vector for each of the 2.2 million sentences in our collection of reports. We then used a method called logistic regression, which learns from examples to estimate how likely something is, to find which sentences described visual effects, based on their vectors. This approach is different from earlier studies of the Erowid reports, which mostly counted how often certain words appeared or how often certain phrases were used (Mooseder et al., 2022; Nayak et al., 2021; Sanz et al., 2018; Zamberlan et al., 2018).

We found that the share of sentences describing visual effects varies a great deal from one substance to another, and that these differences follow a consistent pattern, even among the psychedelics themselves. Next, we read through all the visual effect sentences and sorted them by hand into groups of types of visual experience. For each substance, we then worked out what share of its visual effect sentences fell into each type. We found that the psychedelics consistently differ in their patterns of visual effects.

Overall, our analyses show statistically significant differences in how likely different psychedelics are to affect what people see, and in the other kinds of effects people describe feeling. Our findings also set up a new way to measure and sort the visual effects of substances that affect the mind, and of other altered states of consciousness. Future studies can use our method to describe, in a systematic way, how psychedelics differ in various parts of what people describe feeling. Our method also lays the groundwork for future studies that link measures of the body and brain to numbers describing what people feel. Our results also indicate that the patterns of activity at the docking points on nerve cells that produce the visual effects of psychedelics depend on many factors working together.
parts.methods:
Methods

The Erowid experience reports: our collection of what people describe feeling

The Erowid Center is a nonprofit organization. Its mission is to give the public accurate, unbiased information about substances that affect the mind, free of charge, through its website, Erowid.org (Erowid, 1995–2023). Part of this mission is to tell website visitors what different substances do to them in the short term. For a limited set of substances, the Erowid website already has scientific studies describing both the physical effects and what people describe feeling. But many more substances are used for fun, in ceremonies or as medicine, and their effects have not been well described in carefully controlled experiments. So the Erowid Center collects and keeps a public archive of written reports that people send in, describing their own experiences with these substances.

Any Erowid website user can freely send in a written report about their experience with a substance that affects the mind. Users can also send reports about experiences linked to such substances, or about other altered states of consciousness, such as dreams, meditation, drug testing and run-ins with the police. We left these reports out of our study.

Erowid gives users only a few guidelines for their reports. It asks for clear, well-written descriptions of the experience, including the user's mindset and setting, how much they took and when, the physical and mental effects, how they prepared and what they intended, what they learned, and any problems they had. Erowid Center volunteers then check the reports and remove ones that are clearly made up or exaggerated, or that don't give useful information.

Researchers who work with the Erowid Center can get the report texts, along with extra information about each report, through an application programming interface (API). An API is a way for one computer program to ask another program for information automatically. We used the Erowid API to download the full text of every report about substances that had at least 100 separate reports published between June 13, 1995 and May 22, 2023.

Preparing the text

We first prepared the text data for analysis using the Python programming language. First, we used a tool called Beautiful Soup (Richardson, 2007) to remove the hidden formatting code that the Erowid website uses to display the reports. Next, we split each report into sentences by cutting the text wherever there was a period. We made two exceptions. A period between two numbers was treated as a decimal point, and two periods side by side were treated as an ellipsis (a pause in the writing). We gave each sentence its own sentence number and report number, along with a label for the substance. We left out reports that were linked to more than one substance in the Erowid information.

Our final dataset held reports for 103 substances, 39,586 reports in total, with a middle value (median) of 217 reports per substance. The median number of sentences per report was 40, with a smallest report of 1 sentence and a largest of 1,396. Table 1 summarizes the dataset substance by substance. The substance names in Table 1 and the figures below are exactly as they were entered into the Erowid experience report database. Supplementary Table 1 matches these Erowid names to chemical names or other identifiers.

Turning sentences into lists of numbers

To measure the meaning of the experience reports with numbers, we gave each sentence in the dataset its own list of numbers, called a vector. A text embedding is a way of turning a string of words into a vector, so that how similar two strings are in meaning is linked to how similar their vectors are. Picture each vector as a point in a space with many directions. Two sentences with similar meanings, such as "I sauteed the tofu" and "I braised the bean curd", would sit closer together in this space than two sentences with very different meanings, such as "I sauteed the tofu" and "The president enjoyed my cooking". The distance between two points is called the Euclidean distance.

We made a vector for every sentence in the dataset using a tool from OpenAI called text-embedding-ada-002 (Greene et al., 2022). We calculated these vectors through the OpenAI API between July 10, 2023 and July 23, 2023. The tool turns any piece of text into a vector with 1,536 numbers, one for each of its 1,536 directions. At the time of our analysis, it was the best-performing text embedding tool that OpenAI offered (Greene et al., 2022).

A computer program that picks out sentences about what people see

Erowid experience reports are free-form stories. They often describe the user's mindset and setting, the situation and reasons for taking the substance, how they prepared it and took it, and so on, along with descriptions of the different effects they felt. To compare visual effects across substances in a systematic way, we needed to find the sentences that describe visual effects. But our dataset was too large for anyone to check every sentence by hand. So we built a computer program, called a classifier, that uses the vectors to spot sentences describing visual effects. It is based on logistic regression, a method that learns from examples to estimate how likely something is.

First, we made a set of labeled sentences to train the classifier. We picked 10,000 sentences at random from the dataset, without picking any sentence twice. For each sentence, we asked OpenAI's GPT-4 language model, through its API, to label it as a visual effect sentence or not. We gave GPT-4 this system prompt: "You are a model that identifies effects of psychoactive substances on visual experience (1) or not (0). Classify the following sentence. Respond only with 1 or 0. A 1 means that the sentence explicitly describes a visual effect."

The user prompt for each request was one of the 10,000 sentences, so each sentence got a response of 1 or 0. We set the API's temperature to 0.0, which makes the model as fixed and predictable as possible and lowers the chance of unexpected, "creative" answers. Of the 10,000 sentences we sent to GPT-4, 1,231 (12.31%) were labeled as visual effect sentences and 8,769 (87.69%) as not visual effect sentences.

To check how good this automatic labeling was, we looked through a random sample of 100 sentences that GPT-4 had labeled 0 and 100 that it had labeled 1. One of us (S.N.) decided for each sentence whether it was a visual effect sentence or not, without knowing GPT-4's label. All 100 sentences that GPT-4 had labeled "not visual effect" got the same label in our check. However, 18 of the sentences that GPT-4 had labeled "visual effect" were judged "not visual effect" by our check. So we went through all 1,231 sentences that GPT-4 had labeled "visual effect" and corrected the labels where needed. This lowered the false positive rate, meaning the share of sentences wrongly labeled as visual effects, in the classifier we would later train on the full dataset. In the end, we changed 244 "visual effect" sentences to "not visual effect", leaving 987 "visual effect" sentences and 9,013 "not visual effect" sentences.

We then used a Python tool called Scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) to build a logistic regression classifier from these labeled training sentences. First, we added the matching vectors to the labeled sentences. We then trained the classifier on the vectors, using each of the 1,536 numbers in a vector as an input, and the sentence's label ("not visual effect" or "visual effect") as the answer it had to learn.

We split the data into two parts: 80% for training and 20% for testing. We also took fewer "not visual effect" sentences than "visual effect" sentences from the training part, so that the two groups were equal in size (987 sentences). The classifier's prediction accuracy was 89.3%. We define prediction accuracy as the number of sentences whose labels the classifier produced matched the labels in the training set, divided by the number of sentences in the test set.

Next, we used the trained classifier to estimate how likely each sentence in our full Erowid dataset was to be a visual effect sentence. We looked through a sample of these classified sentences to see whether the classifier's estimates matched our own judgments of "visual effect" versus "not visual effect" sentences.

Table 2 shows example sentences and the classifier's probability for each one. We found that the probability generally matched how sure we were that a sentence described a visual effect. Based on our review, we chose a cutoff probability of 0.75: a sentence with a probability of 0.75 or more counted as a visual effect sentence. We chose this cutoff to keep false positives low. In total, 143,520 sentences were above this cutoff, which is 6.52% of all the sentences in the full dataset.

Figure 1 shows how the probabilities are spread out for all the sentences in the dataset and for a selection of single substances. Most sentences have a probability below 0.5. We expected this, because Erowid reports often describe many more parts of a substance experience than just visual effects. Figure 1 shows the spread of probabilities for the four substances with the most reports and the four with the fewest. (To be included in our analysis, a substance needed at least 100 reports.) The overall shape of the spread is similar across substances, and most of the differences between substances appear at the high end of the probabilities. We look at these differences more closely below.

Figure 1

Histograms showing how often each probability value appears for selected substances. In each small chart, the horizontal axis shows the probability and the vertical axis shows how often that probability appears. Because the substances have different numbers of sentences in their reports, the vertical axes are scaled so that the highest value sits at the top of each chart. The red line in each chart shows the spread of probabilities for the whole dataset. The trained classifier calculated the probability for each sentence.

Sorting visual effects into types

In this study, we asked whether experience reports from people who use psychedelics and other substances that affect the mind differ in a consistent way in how they describe visual effects. To answer this, we first used the trained classifier to pull out the sentences that describe visual effects from the original reports. We made a new dataset of visual effect sentences: every sentence whose probability was at least 0.75, together with its substance label and its vector. We then used the vectors to measure how the types of visual effects are spread out for each substance.

The vectors turn how similar two sentences are in meaning into a distance between points in a space. So we used them to measure, for each substance, the share of its sentences that describe each type of visual effect. To decide which types to study, we first explored the whole range of visual effect meanings. We did this by flattening the many-number vectors onto a flat, two-dimensional map, using a method called uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP). UMAP is designed to keep both the big-picture and the small-scale structure of data with many numbers that change in curved, not straight-line, ways (McInnes et al., 2018).

This two-dimensional UMAP map helps us see how the visual effect sentences relate to one another in meaning. It also helps us find typical sentences, which we call seed sentences, that stand for different regions of the map. One of us (SN) walked through the map, reading many sentences spread across it, to explore the range of meanings. Based on this walk, the same author (SN) then wrote typical sentences by hand to represent the common kinds of visual effect descriptions found in the reports. Figure 2 shows this process, and Table 3 lists the seed sentences we wrote, which we used as starting points for the rest of the analysis.

Figure 2

(A) A two-dimensional UMAP map of all the visual effect sentence vectors. Each dot is one visual effect sentence, and colors show different substances. Arrows point to some example sentences. (B) How we sorted the visual effects and calculated them. We wrote seed sentences (listed in Table 3) to represent different regions of the map. Each visual effect was the area within a set distance of a seed sentence's vector. We then compared the share of visual effect sentences that fell into each type across substances. The black circles on the map show how we did this: each circle is centered on a seed sentence's vector, and we counted sentences within a set distance. The analysis was done in the original space of 1,536 numbers; the two-dimensional map with circles shown here is only for illustration.

We wrote these sentences to be typical of the different types of visual effects we saw in the full set of visual effect sentences, and we then used them as seed sentences for sorting the visual effects into types.

To measure how likely a given substance is to cause each type of visual effect, we counted the share of that substance's visual effect sentences whose vectors fell within a set distance of each seed sentence. We chose a distance cutoff of 0.55, based on looking through the report sentences and measuring how far they sat from the seed sentences. We decided that this is roughly the distance beyond which a sentence is no longer similar enough in meaning to the seed sentence to count as an example of that type of visual effect. Figure 2 shows this distance method on a two-dimensional UMAP map, although the real calculation uses all 1,536 numbers in each vector. Figure 3 shows the whole method as a flowchart.

Figure 3

Flowchart of how we calculated the spread of visual effects across substances from the Erowid experience report dataset.

To test whether the differences between psychedelic substances in their mix of visual effect types were statistically significant, we used a permutation test. A permutation test shuffles the data many times to see how often a difference as large as the real one appears by chance alone. Our test used a number, called T, that measures how much the substances differ in how they relate to the seed sentences. For each seed sentence, we compared every pair of substances and took the average size of the difference between their shares of sentences. This shows how spread out the substances are in how they relate to that seed sentence. We repeated this for every seed sentence, and T is the average of these differences. In short, T sums up how much the substances vary in how they relate to the whole range of visual effect types.

In symbols, T is defined as:

T = (1/|S|) × Σ_{s∈S} (2/|D|) × Σ_{d1,d2∈D; d1≠d2} |V(s,d1) − V(s,d2)|

Where:

S is the set of all seed sentences,

D is the set of all substances,

V(s,d) is the value for seed sentence s and substance d (the share of that substance's visual effect sentences within the distance cutoff),

|S| and |D| are the numbers of seed sentences and substances.

In this formula, the inner sum is the average size of the difference between every pair of substances for seed sentence s. The outer sum is the average of these averages across all seed sentences.

We wrote the seed sentences to match the types of visual effect sentences we often came across while reading through the list of visual effect sentences, arranged by how similar they were on the two-dimensional UMAP map. So we chose the seed sentences from our own judgment, rather than letting the data pick them. In future work, a method that finds the types of visual effect from the data alone, without people sorting them, would allow a more objective study of consistent differences in the visual effects of different psychedelics. For this study, however, we reasoned that types of visual effect chosen by hand, if they showed statistically significant differences, would let us test for differences in the visual effects of different psychedelics.
parts.results:
Results

The share of sentences that described visual effects differed between substances, and these differences were statistically significant (Figure 4). To check this, we used a chi-square test. This test asks whether two things are linked. Here, the two things were the substance a report was about and whether its sentences described visual effects. Our starting assumption, called the null hypothesis, was that the two are not linked at all: that the share of visual effect sentences would be the same for every substance. We rejected that assumption. The test gave X2 (114, N = 2,246,254) = 72,912, p < 0.001. The p-value means that if there were really no link, a pattern this strong would turn up by chance less than 0.1% of the time.

We also measured how strong the link was, using a score called Cramér's V. It runs from 0, meaning no link at all, to 1, meaning the two things are completely tied together. For all the sentences in our report collection, the score was 0.180. That counts as a small-to-moderate link.

Psychedelics tended to have a much higher share of visual effect sentences than any other group of drugs. We compared the two groups directly with a two-sample t-test, a standard way to compare the averages of two groups. Psychedelics had a statistically significantly higher share of visual effect sentences than the other substances (p < 0.001).

Figure 4

The share of sentences that described visual effects for each substance that affects the mind. Colors show which group of drugs each substance belongs to.

The share of visual effect sentences also differed significantly between substances when we looked only at the psychedelics (Figure 5). The chi-square test gave X2 (29, N = 931,858) = 5,771, p < 0.001. This time, Cramér's V was 0.078, which points to a small link.

Figure 5

The share of sentences that described visual effects for each psychedelic. Colors show which group of drugs each psychedelic belongs to.

The results in Figures 4 and 5 show that the share of visual effect sentences varies reliably, both across all substances and across the psychedelics alone. We also sorted the visual effect sentences into types of effect (see Methods). This showed that the share of each type of effect also varies from one psychedelic to another.

We show these results in a clustermap (Figure 6). A clustermap is a grid of colored squares, called a heatmap, with tree-shaped diagrams, called dendrograms, along its edges. Each row of the grid is one seed sentence, and each column is one substance. A seed sentence is a sample sentence that we used as a reference point. The colors show the share of each type of visual effect. The dendrograms arrange the seed sentences and the substances so that the most similar ones sit close together. Each leaf of a dendrogram stands for one item, which is one row or one column of the heatmap. Branches join the leaves. To measure how different two leaves are, you count how many branch crossings you must travel between them. The more crossings, the more different the two items are, within the group they belong to (either the seed sentences or the psychedelics) (Figure 6).

Figure 6

Clustermap of the share of each type of visual effect for each psychedelic. For each seed sentence, we worked out the share of visual effect sentences for each psychedelic that fell within a set distance of the seed sentence's meaning vector. This share measures how strongly a report sentence is linked to a given seed sentence, and the colors on the right of the figure show it. The map combines a heatmap with dendrograms, which group the substances and the visual effect sentences by how similar they are. In the dendrograms, the total branch distance between two leaves (seed sentences or substances) shows how different those two leaves are. Substance labels are colored by the chemical group of the psychedelic, and seed sentence labels are colored by the type of sentence.

To measure how different two substances, or two seed sentences, are, we used the Euclidean distance between their lists of shares. You can picture this as the straight-line distance between two points on a map. The clustermap shows three clear groups of seed sentences across all substances: those with fairly high shares, those with medium shares and those with low shares (Figure 6). These three groups do not match the types of sentence that we sorted by hand. For example, the high-share group includes seed sentences about color, movement and pattern, but these types also appear in the other two groups (Figure 6).

Looking at the picture, the longest branches in the seed-sentence dendrogram separate the seed sentences into three groups. This suggests that the overall share of visual effect sentences is the most important factor in how the seed sentences group together.

The dendrogram for the psychedelics tells a different story. It does not separate the substances into clearly distinct groups, as clearly as it does for the seed sentences (Figure 6). It suggests that the psychedelics fall into three main clusters. However, the branches that split these three clusters are shorter than the branches that split the three seed-sentence clusters. This suggests that the shares of visual effect sentences differ less between the substances in the three clusters than they do between the seed sentences in the three clusters.

Next, we wanted to test whether the psychedelics differ from one another in how strongly they are linked to the seed sentences. To do this, we created a test score called T (see Methods). It measures how much the psychedelics differ from one another in the strength of their links to the seed sentences. For our collection of visual effect sentences, T was 0.0165.

To see what T would look like if there were no real link between substance and visual effect pattern, we shuffled the substance labels in the data. We then worked out T again for the shares from this shuffled data. This gave us a null distribution: a set of T values that we would expect to see if the labels were just randomly mixed up.

We repeated this shuffling and T calculation 10,000 times. This gave us a range of T values that we could expect if there were no link between substance and visual effect pattern. We then found the p-value: the share of the shuffled T values that were as large as, or larger than, the real T value. This p-value was less than 0.001. It shows that the psychedelics differ from one another in a statistically significant and consistent way in how they relate to the seed sentences.
parts.discussion:
Discussion

We found that experience reports about different psychedelic substances differ in how many of their sentences describe each type of visual effect (Figure 6). This suggests that the pattern of visual effects for any one psychedelic depends on many factors. That would support the idea that the way psychedelics change what we see also depends on many factors. In other words, it would support the idea that these effects cannot be explained by a substance acting on just one type, or one subtype, of receptor.

One receptor that has drawn a lot of attention is the 5-HT2A receptor. It belongs to the family of serotonin receptors, which respond to the chemical messenger serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT). Researchers have proposed that this receptor is what produces the effects of psychedelics on how people feel. Classical psychedelics such as DMT, LSD, psilocybin and mescaline are sometimes called serotonergic psychedelics, meaning "serotonin psychedelics", because they attach to serotonin receptors, especially the 5-HT2A subtype (Nichols, 2016). The 5-HT2A receptor has been described as necessary for some effects of classical psychedelics. These include people's ratings of complex visual images and increased excitability of the visual cortex, meaning that the part of the brain that processes what we see becomes more easily stirred into activity (Kometer et al., 2013; Preller et al., 2018; Quednow et al., 2012). On top of that, 5-HT2A receptors are packed densely into the visual cortex (Beliveau et al., 2017).

Our results fit with the idea that switching on the 5-HT2A receptor does not, on its own, decide what a person sees under a psychedelic. Suppose that psychedelics differed only in how strongly they attach to 5-HT2A receptors, or in how much they switch them on. Then we would expect the strength of their effects to change with the dose, and the pattern of effects would be more similar from one psychedelic to another. This would be especially true for two substances that attach to the 5-HT2A receptor about equally strongly and switch it on about equally much. Instead, our results suggest that different psychedelics have their own typical mix of visual effects, and that this mix is linked to the substance in a statistically significant way.

Some studies have used a drug called ketanserin, which blocks the 5-HT2A receptor. Researchers have read their results as meaning that switching on this receptor may be necessary for the typical effects of psychedelics (Kometer et al., 2013; Preller et al., 2018; Quednow et al., 2012). However, scientists have found several substances that switch on the 5-HT2A receptor but are not themselves psychedelics. For example, lisuride and ergotamine are chemical relatives of LSD. They have been described as non-psychedelic because the effects people feel from them do not look like the effects usually linked with psychedelics (González-Maeso et al., 2007; Pieri et al., 1978). Yet when researchers measured how much these drugs switch on the receptor, they found that they do so about as much as their psychedelic relatives (Bonhaus et al., 1997; Egan et al., 1998). So the existence of these non-psychedelic substances that switch on 5-HT2A receptors points to one of two possibilities. Either switching on this receptor is not enough by itself to cause visual effects. Or there is a threshold, a certain level of activation that must be reached, before a psychedelic effect appears in a particular chain of signals inside the cell or in a particular group of nerve cells (Wallach et al., 2023).

There is more. Recent evidence shows that ketanserin does more than block the 5-HT2A receptor. It also attaches, to a moderate degree, to another serotonin receptor subtype, the 5-HT2C receptor. It also attaches, to a moderate to high degree, to several receptors that respond to adrenaline-like messengers and to histamine, the messenger involved in allergies (Casey et al., 2022). So the full set of effects that any given psychedelic produces is likely to depend on how it switches on many types of serotonin receptors and other kinds of receptors, not just on how much it switches on the 5-HT2A receptor.

In our full set of experience reports, the share of sentences that described visual effects differed in a statistically significant way across all substances (Figure 4). It also differed in a statistically significant way among the psychedelics themselves (Figure 5). These differences show how likely each substance is to cause visual effects compared with other kinds of effects. Notably, psychedelics had a significantly larger share of visual effect sentences than the non-psychedelic substances. This was true even though reports about psychedelics also generally tended to contain more sentences overall (Table 1). The Erowid experience reports are free-form and nobody asks people to answer particular questions. So whether someone describes an effect in a report probably reflects how striking or memorable that effect was for them.

We found that the pattern of visual effects depends on many factors, and that psychedelics differ in how likely they are to cause visual effects. We also know from drug research that different psychedelic substances attach to different types of receptors with different strengths (Jensen and Roth, 2008). Taken together, these findings suggest that switching on many types of receptors is important for explaining what people see under any given psychedelic. Other researchers have described this possibility before. For example, some have suggested that switching on the 5-HT1A receptor may have larger effects on how the brain processes what we see than switching on the 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors (Nichols, 2000). However, there is not yet a clearly established link between receptor types or subtypes and how likely a substance is to cause visual effects, or what kinds of visual effects it causes.

There are other possible reasons why substances that switch on the 5-HT2A receptor could cause different visual effects. One is that different substances may carry the receptor to different places inside the cell (Berg et al., 1998). Another is that a substance may switch on some of the receptor's signaling chains more strongly than others, which is called biased agonism. A third is that the substances people swallow are broken down into other chemicals, called metabolites, which may also act on the body.

To measure how big these differences were, we used a statistic called Cramér's V. It shows how strongly a set of categories, here the types of substances, is linked to another set of categories, here the share of visual effect sentences. A value near 0 means almost no link, and larger values mean a stronger link. Across all substances, the share of visual effect sentences varied with a small-to-moderate effect size. When we looked only at the psychedelics, the effect size was small. The larger effect size across all substances comes from the fact that different groups of drugs differ in how likely they are to cause visual effects. Psychedelics were the most likely, and opioids were the least likely (Figure 4).

Our study shows how useful it is to analyze large collections of written reports in which people describe their own experiences, when studying what substances that affect the mind do to people. A single substance can cause a wide range of visual effects that vary a lot, both from one person to another and within the same person. So we need large, high-quality collections of reports, such as Erowid's Experience Vaults. Only then can we work out accurately how likely each substance is to cause each kind of visual effect, and have enough data to compare these patterns with one another in a meaningful way. As far as we know, our study is the first to use numbers to show that different psychedelic substances lead to different kinds of visual experiences.

The way we studied written text with numbers is a step forward in method. It combines the strengths of computer analysis of language with careful reading and interpretation of text. We used a tool from OpenAI that turns each sentence into a list of numbers (called text-embedding-ada-002; Greene et al., 2022). It works so that sentences with similar meanings get lists of numbers that are also similar. We then used another OpenAI tool, the GPT-4 large language model, to automatically build a set of examples with known answers, which we used to train our classifier.

By combining these two kinds of tools, we found the visual effect sentences in the Erowid collection on a large scale. This took little research effort, and we did not have to worry about whether different people would have labeled the same sentences in the same way. Our method has several steps. First, every piece of text in a collection, such as each sentence, is turned into a list of numbers. Next, a set of training examples is built automatically. Finally, a classifier labels every piece of text. This approach could be used in many ways to study experience reports about substances that affect the mind, and in other fields too.

Differences in the visual reports we analyzed might partly come from things other than the drugs themselves. First, how striking different parts of a visual effect seem could depend on non-visual influences, such as changes in thinking. In future work, we can extend our method to the non-visual parts of the psychedelic experience to look into this possibility. Second, the situation people were in, and differences between groups of people, also shape the reports. If different substances tend to be used in different situations and settings, or by different groups of people, these differences might show up as differences in visual effects in our results. These challenges are built into any observational study that relies on people describing their own experiences of substances they took themselves. In future work, our method could be used in research studies where the situation, the setting and the group of people are more carefully controlled.

In future work, our method for studying the patterns of visual effects that psychedelics produce could be combined with chemical and body measurements. These include how strongly a substance attaches to receptors, how much it switches them on, and brain activity. In general, the effects of psychedelics on what we are aware of, and on brain activity as a whole, cannot be boiled down directly to how strongly a substance attaches to receptors. Different substances that attach to the same receptor can cause different patterns of activity in the brain for many reasons. These include differences in how strongly they attach, effects that do not grow in simple step with the amount of attachment, threshold effects, and whether the substance switches the receptor on or blocks it. Even so, our method for measuring the effects of psychedelics on what people describe feeling can be combined with chemical, anatomical, body and psychological measurements. Together, these could help us learn more about how psychedelics act in the brain and about the biological basis of what we see while we are awake.
